# The Reality of Exposing PHP Source Code on Apache2

The short answer is yes, PHP source code is trivially visible to anyone who can reach your web server unless you take specific steps to prevent it. This isn't a matter of security through obscurity or complex encryption; it is a direct consequence of how the PHP engine operates within an Apache environment. When Apache invokes the PHP interpreter, that interpreter executes your logic and generates an output stream (HTML, JSON, etc.) which is sent back to the browser. By default, this process discards the source code. However, if you misconfigure your server, you can accidentally disable the "output buffering" or "code stripping" mechanisms, effectively serving the raw `.php` file as plain text.

This specific vulnerability is often introduced by a single configuration error in `httpd.conf` or `.htaccess`. If you have uncommented the line `ExposePhp On`, your server will serve the source code directly to any client that requests a `.php` resource. Similarly, enabling `PrintEnvironmentVariableDescriptions` can leak sensitive data, while `DisplayErrors On` might expose stack traces containing file paths and variable values that aid an attacker in mapping your application structure.

To remediate this on your Ubuntu 9.10 Apache2 setup, you must audit these settings. Open your main configuration file or the relevant virtual host definition and ensure the following directives are set correctly:

```apache
<IfModule mod_php5.c>
    ExposePhp Off
    PrintEnvironmentVariableDescriptions Off
    DisplayErrors Off
    LogErrors On
</IfModule>
```

Disabling `ExposePhp` is the critical step here. It tells Apache to explicitly strip PHP tags and serve only the rendered output. If you are running a legacy environment like Ubuntu 9.10 with PHP 5, relying on default behaviors can be risky because older defaults often leaned towards verbose error reporting for debugging purposes, which inadvertently aids attackers once production is live.

Beyond server configuration, there is a fundamental architectural distinction between "displaying code" and "exposing logic." Even if you successfully hide the source files via file permissions (setting `chmod 640` on your PHP files so only the web user can read them) or placing them outside the document root, you cannot physically protect the business logic contained within that code. The entire reason for using PHP is that the server executes it before sending anything to the client.

If an attacker knows how to interact with your application's API endpoints, they can infer the existence of functions and classes by analyzing response times or error messages. For instance, if you have a `user.php` file that handles authentication, and you accidentally set `display_errors=1`, an attacker sending a malformed request will see a stack trace revealing exactly which libraries are included and what database credentials might be hardcoded in variable dumps.

The most robust defense against source code leakage is strict adherence to the separation of concerns. Never commit your production-ready PHP files to public repositories without stripping sensitive keys, and never deploy them with `display_errors` enabled. Instead, utilize a custom error handler that logs exceptions to a file accessible only by the server administrator while returning generic "500 Internal Server Error" responses to users.

If you are building or maintaining a larger application stack and need to manage dependencies, security patches, and deployment workflows more efficiently, platforms like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) offer tools and resources that can help streamline these processes while enforcing modern security standards out of the box.
